headline: After seeing Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump's envoys head to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelensky
standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spent more than two hours at the Kremlin before heading to Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. Israel is reportedly readying a strike on Iran, Ebola passes 11,000 cases in DR Congo, António Guterres urges COP31 to be done with fossil fuels, and clashes are reported on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border.

essentials.title: After seeing Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump's envoys head to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelensky
essentials.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spent more than two hours at the Kremlin on Thursday, with nothing announced on the substance of the conflict. Moscow says they backed a humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka.
body: On Thursday 12 November Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, received America's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, at the Kremlin for more than two hours, a day after two days of three-way talks in Abu Dhabi ended in a prisoner-exchange deal, according to TASS and ABC News.

The Kremlin's foreign-policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, called the meeting “constructive” and said the Americans supported a Russian proposal for a humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka, in the Donetsk region, and that the three-way talks would continue, but said nothing on territory, which Moscow demands and Kyiv refuses to cede.

The two envoys are expected in Dublin on Thursday evening to see Volodymyr Zelensky, who doubts they will bring back “something concrete”, while a Russian drone strike on a block of flats in Kyiv killed a woman and injured seven people that morning, according to Meduza and ABC News.

figure.label: drones detected overnight over the Baltic states, according to Vilnius
figure.compare: one alert covered Kaunas and its 300,000 or so residents

positions.wants: Recognition of its conquests in eastern Ukraine, and no Europeans in the direct talks.
“Concrete mechanisms” against any resumption of the war, no surrender of the Donbas, and Europe involved at every stage.
A breakthrough that “will take time”, according to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who called the first session “very productive”.

analysis.title: The Baltic, the war's blind spot
analysis.text: Ukraine's strikes on Russia's Baltic oil ports regularly spill over into neighbouring countries: Ukrainian drones have already strayed into Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Reuters notes. Moscow accuses Kyiv of using NATO airspace as cover; Kyiv says Russian jamming knocks its drones off course. On the night of 10-11 November an attempt was made to shoot down a drone over northern Lithuania, and debris from a NATO missile was found on the ground, though it is unclear whether the drone was hit. Finland, for its part, temporarily restricted its airspace and waters in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

keys.title: The prisoner exchange
keys.text: Russia's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, and his Ukrainian counterpart, Rustem Umerov, both confirmed the planned swap, which they described as “significant”. The talks also covered detained civilians and children taken from Ukraine, according to the AP.

keys.title: The strikes go on
keys.text: Russia's defence ministry claims to have shot down 627 Ukrainian drones in a single night. In Ukraine, a Russian strike cut power to Kryvyi Rih and injured people in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia, according to Reuters, which could not verify the reports.

context.t: Russia launches its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

essentials.title: Israel is reportedly readying a strike on Iran as two supertankers explode in Hormuz
essentials.standfirst: Israel's security cabinet has reportedly ordered the army to step up preparations for an attack, according to the public broadcaster Kan. In Hormuz, the Revolutionary Guards say two supertankers were disabled by explosions.
body: On the evening of Wednesday 11 November Israel's security cabinet, chaired by the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the army to step up preparations for an attack on Iran, according to the public broadcaster Kan, cited by Al Jazeera, even as Gadi Eisenkot urged him not to deploy the army without a direct and immediate threat.

That same night two supertankers were disabled by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings, the Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday, threatening the same fate for any ship that co-operates with the American armed forces, according to Reuters.

Donald Trump says he is ready to return to war if Qatar's mediation fails, even though his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, thinks the blockade effective enough to make that unnecessary, and Brent closed at $92.76 on Wednesday after Tehran rejected moving its enriched uranium to a third country, according to Al Jazeera.

figure.label: a barrel of Brent on 11 November, according to Al Jazeera
figure.compare: against $71 on 27 February, the eve of the war, according to the EIA

positions.wants: Keep up the blockade and impose “devastating” economic costs on Iran while professing openness to diplomacy; Marco Rubio calls Iran's demands “totally unrealistic”.
The lifting of sanctions and of the blockade, a smaller American military presence, restored oil waivers and the release of its frozen assets; no transfer of enriched uranium.
A diplomatic solution, which its prime minister still considers possible, with “cautious optimism”.

impact.text: A barrel of Brent closed at $92.76 on 11 November, according to Al Jazeera, against $71 on the eve of the war, according to America's Energy Information Administration: a rise of nearly a third, which makes fuel dearer and, in turn, the cost of getting about.

analysis.title: A divided administration
analysis.text: According to Reuters, the new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, and the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, favour economic pressure, while J.D. Vance prefers a deal. At the G7, Marco Rubio reportedly called Iran's leaders “crazy”, according to two diplomats. The strategy worries countries such as Pakistan, Iraq and Turkey, which bear its economic cost, Al Jazeera notes. A Reuters/Ipsos poll finds that 71% of Americans support legislation to end the war. In Iran, the rial has lost more than half its value against the dollar in a year, according to Iran International, and the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, insists that neither force nor sanctions will end the conflict.

keys.title: The strait under pressure
keys.text: Since the war began Tehran has required ships to follow authorised routes, while Washington escorts tankers and blockades Iran's ports. India's shipping minister reported a Liberian-flagged tanker hit by a projectile in the Gulf, with four sailors injured.

keys.title: Threats in the West
keys.text: America's Justice Department has charged three alleged Iranian agents over plots to carry out attacks in America and Europe. Scott Bessent has moved onto a military base after threats attributed to Iran, according to the New York Times.

context.t: War breaks out between America, Israel and Iran.
Iran proposes a seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz and resume talks.
Midterm elections, lost by the Republicans.
Marco Rubio rules out new major operations; three tankers ablaze, according to the Guards.
A tanker strikes a mine; that night two supertankers explode in Hormuz and Israel readies an attack, according to Kan.

essentials.title: Ebola in DR Congo passes 11,000 confirmed cases and 5,300 deaths
essentials.standfirst: Figures published on Tuesday by the Congolese government confirm an outbreak of exceptional scale, the second-largest ever recorded. No vaccine or treatment is approved against the Bundibugyo strain.
body: According to figures published by the Congolese government on Tuesday 10 November, the Ebola outbreak declared in mid-May in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo now stands at 11,042 confirmed cases and 5,387 deaths, the worst in the country's history, Reuters and the AP report.

Caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved, it has reached eight of the country's 26 provinces, above all Ituri and North Kivu, where insecurity hampers access to treatment centres and many patients die at home, according to Reuters.

It is the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, after West Africa's in 2014-2016, and the vaccine trial launched in Bunia at the end of October is not expected to produce results before 2027, while Kenya has recorded nine cases and Nigeria one imported case.

items.note: Capital of Ituri, the worst-hit province; the Tumaini vaccine trial began here on 23 October.

impact.text: For people living in the European Union, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control rates the risk of infection as “very low”; it remains “low” for those living in or travelling to the affected areas, from which a few sick health workers have been flown home.

analysis.title: An outbreak outrunning the response
analysis.text: According to the WHO, 512 people died between 21 October and 3 November, 335 of them outside treatment centres, a sign that many patients are slipping through the health system. Daily follow-up of contacts reached only 86%, short of the 95% target, and transmission remained active in 51 health zones. The organisation, which declared the outbreak a public-health emergency of international concern as early as 17 May, reports serious funding gaps. The fatality rate, close to 49%, is in line with that of a 2012 outbreak in DR Congo caused by the same strain. The Tumaini trial is testing, among others, two vaccines designed against the Bundibugyo virus, one by the University of Oxford and one by Moderna.

keys.title: Ituri and North Kivu
keys.text: As of 9 November Ituri had recorded 7,654 cases and 3,613 deaths, and North Kivu 2,720 cases and 1,488 deaths, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Both eastern provinces are also the scene of armed conflicts.

keys.title: Beyond the borders
keys.text: Uganda overcame its outbreak this summer, after 20 cases. Kenya has recorded no new case since 19 October, and the patient diagnosed in Nigeria was evacuated to Geneva.

essentials.title: At COP31, António Guterres urges world leaders to be done with fossil fuels
essentials.standfirst: Addressing the leaders' summit in Antalya, the UN secretary-general said a temporary overshoot of 1.5°C was now inevitable. He wants an end to new coal, oil and gas projects.
body: On Wednesday 11 November, addressing the COP31 leaders' summit in Antalya, Turkey, the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, said that overshooting the 1.5°C warming threshold was “now inevitable” and called for an end to all new coal, oil and gas projects.

Global emissions would need to fall by about 6% a year, whereas national plans deliver a third of that at best and point to more than 2.5°C of warming by the end of the century, he said, before proposing a tax on oil companies' windfall profits.

Brazil's president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, lamented that climate had vanished from G7 and G20 speeches, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian demanded compensation for the environmental damage done by wars, and the negotiations, led by Australia, are due to end on 20 November.

figure.label: of warming by 2100 if national plans are carried out
figure.compare: against the 1.5°C goal of the Paris agreement

positions.wants: No new coal and no new oil or gas infrastructure, and at least $300bn a year in climate finance by 2035.
“Common but differentiated” responsibilities: rich countries should cut their emissions first and keep their finance promises, according to its vice-president, Han Zheng.
A global commitment to electrification, championed by the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
New and predictable climate finance, paid as grants, according to President Mohamed Muizzu.

items.name: Antalya
items.note: Host city of COP31 and of the leaders' summit on 11 and 12 November.

analysis.title: The numbers of a farewell speech
analysis.text: António Guterres, who leaves office next year, set two realities side by side. On one hand, emissions hit a record in 2025 and the past four years were the hottest ever measured. On the other, solar power met nearly three-quarters of the growth in global electricity demand last year, and almost one car in three sold this year will be electric. He pointed out that the nine biggest oil companies made $95bn in profits in the last quarter, while the loss-and-damage fund has received only about $600m. He proposes a “climate justice pact” built on a just transition, protecting people, finance and co-operation.

keys.title: The Turkish host
keys.text: Turkey's president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, pleaded for more solidarity in the face of wars, crises and migration. Turkey is hosting the conference, while Australia is leading the negotiations.

keys.title: The solar pledges
keys.text: Australia, Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu have signed a declaration that aims to double, by 2030, the number of households with rooftop solar panels, according to the AP.

context.t: Adoption of the Paris agreement, which aims to limit warming to 1.5°C.

essentials.title: In northern Tigray, Ethiopia's army and Eritrean forces are reported to be clashing around Badme
essentials.standfirst: Having retaken most of Tigray in October, the federal army is pushing towards the Eritrean border. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of invasion; Asmara calls that a pretext for war.
body: On Monday 9 November Ethiopia's federal army and Eritrean forces reportedly clashed around Badme, a long-disputed border town, according to observers cited by the Critical Threats Project, which could not confirm it, after the Ethiopian army took Sheraro and Adi Awala on 3 November.

Since late September federal troops, allied with a breakaway Tigrayan faction, have been fighting the forces of the Tigray People's Liberation Front, and Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of an “invasion” reaching 60km into Tigray, which Asmara portrays as a pretext for a war of aggression.

The prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, who regards his country's access to the Red Sea as inevitable, installed an interim government in Tigray in mid-October, while Chinese envoys were received in Addis Ababa in early November and then by Eritrea's president, Isaias Afwerki, in an effort to avert open war.

analysis.title: The Red Sea in the background
analysis.text: Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of preparing a war of aggression ever since Abiy Ahmed laid claim, in 2023, to access to the sea, notably via the Eritrean port of Assab. Returned to power in October, the prime minister has repeated that such access is “only a matter of time”. In October the federal army retook Shire, Axum, Adwa, Adigrat and then Zalambessa, held by Eritrea since 2022, according to the Critical Threats Project. Ethiopia's foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, has taken the matter to the Security Council; his Eritrean counterpart said the letter amounted to a declaration of war. The two countries already fought each other from 1998 to 2000, in a border war that killed tens of thousands.

keys.title: Tigray under supervision
keys.text: Installed on 16 October, Tigray's interim government brings together figures backed by Addis Ababa. More than 5,000 former Tigrayan fighters are going through a disarmament programme in Mekelle, according to state media.

keys.title: The other fronts
keys.text: The army is also fighting Fano militias in Amhara, where it retook several towns in early November. Sudan, for its part, accuses Ethiopia of letting the Rapid Support Forces launch drones from its territory.

brief.text: Israel's new Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday; Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff who has six weeks to form a government, promises to undo much of the policy of the outgoing prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

At least 300 schools were evacuated on Wednesday after emailed bomb threats, which also targeted the prime minister, Giorgia Meloni; the education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, sees in them “a strategy”.

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, the country's highest court of appeal, unanimously struck down colonial-era laws criminalising gay sex on Tuesday, ending a case brought by Jason Jones in 2017.
